messages.content:
Given a question and an answer, analyze the complexity of each sentence in the answer. Break down each sentence into one or more fully understandable statements. Ensure that no pronouns are used in any statement. Format the outputs in JSON.
Please return the output in a JSON format that complies with the following schema as specified in JSON Schema:
{"properties": {"statements": {"description": "The generated statements", "items": {"type": "string"}, "title": "Statements", "type": "array"}}, "required": ["statements"], "title": "StatementGeneratorOutput", "type": "object"}Do not use single quotes in your response but double quotes,properly escaped with a backslash.

--------EXAMPLES-----------
Example 1
Input: {
    "question": "Who was Albert Einstein and what is he best known for?",
    "answer": "He was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. He was best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics."
}
Output: {
    "statements": [
        "Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist.",
        "Albert Einstein is recognized as one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time.",
        "Albert Einstein was best known for developing the theory of relativity.",
        "Albert Einstein also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics."
    ]
}
-----------------------------

Now perform the same with the following input
input: {
    "question": "user: What is the difference between Calico policy Description and Kubernetes policy Description?\nassistant: The Calico policy Description refers to the policies that are specific to the Calico network plugin in a Kubernetes cluster. These policies are used to manage and control network traffic in the cluster, allowing or blocking traffic based on network interfaces, pod sources or destinations, and Kubernetes services.\nOn the other hand, Kubernetes policy Description refers to the policies that are built into Kubernetes and limit access to the Kubernetes Dashboard. These policies are applied at the pod level and affect all classic and VPC clusters. They are used to block all pods from accessing the Kubernetes Dashboard or the dashboard metrics scraper, unless the pod is deployed in a namespace that has the appropriate labels.\nIn summary, Calico policies are focused on managing and controlling network traffic, while Kubernetes policies are focused on limiting access to the Kubernetes Dashboard.\nuser: How does Calico enforce policies?",
    "answer": "Calico policies allow or block network traffic on specific network interfaces, regardless of the Kubernetes pod source or destination IP address or CIDR. [S10] They support advanced controls, such as blocking inbound (ingress) traffic to network load balancer (NLB) services. [S7] Calico policies can be applied using the `calicoctl` command line. [S9]\n\nThe document describes these policy capabilities but does not explain Calico’s underlying enforcement mechanism."
}
Output:

response_text:
{
  "statements": [
    "Calico policies allow or block network traffic on specific network interfaces.",
    "Calico policies allow or block network traffic regardless of the Kubernetes pod source or destination IP address or CIDR.",
    "Calico policies support advanced traffic controls.",
    "Calico policies can block inbound (ingress) traffic to network load balancer (NLB) services.",
    "Calico policies can be applied using the calicoctl command line.",
    "The document describes Calico policy capabilities.",
    "The document does not explain the underlying enforcement mechanism used by Calico."
  ]
}
